docs.title: Nectar Apps
docs.text:
Deploy any app to your own server in three clicks. Pick a type — Java JAR, native binary, static site, Node.js, Python, PHP or a Docker image — pick a runtime version and upload. The app runs in its own Kubernetes namespace and is live at myapp.yourdomain.com behind nectar-gateway, with HTTPS from Let's Encrypt.

Early development

Deploys, Git builds, domains, alerts, databases, backups, updates and the web terminal work, but they have not yet been tested on many real servers. Expect rough edges.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text: One install install.sh sets up k3s, nectar-gateway (ports 80/443) and the panel on a Linux server — or moves into a k3s server you already run (adopt mode). Apps without Dockerfiles Upload a JAR, a binary, a zip of your site — the panel runs it on an official runtime image. Or deploy any image, or build from Git. Domains and HTTPS Every app gets <app>-<project>.<base domain>; add your own domains, redirects, IP allowlists, CORS, HSTS. Wildcard certificates and automatic Cloudflare DNS records. Databases PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Redis per project, linked to apps with DATABASE_URL. Operations Logs (live + searchable history), metrics, a web terminal, volume file browser, alerts (ntfy, Telegram, email, webhooks, native push), restic backups, one-click updates with rollback. Teams Users, roles per project, API tokens, two-factor authentication, single sign-on (GitHub, Google, OIDC). Automation nectar CLI, a GitHub Action, nectar.yaml blueprints, docker-compose import, a full HTTP API. Apps on your phone The Flutter app (Android, iOS, macOS) is the same UI as the web panel.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
internet ──► nectar-gateway (80/443, Let's Encrypt, rate limits, health checks)
                                │   routes + certificates pushed by the panel
                                ▼
   nectar-apps panel ──► k3s: one namespace per project ──► your apps, databases, volumes
   (Go + SQLite, web UI)          Deployments · Services · PVCs · CronJobs · Jobs
  • The panel (nectar-apps, Go, SQLite) is the source of truth: it renders Kubernetes objects with server-side apply and labels everything it owns. It never touches objects it did not create unless you adopt them.
  • The gateway (nectar-gateway) is a reverse proxy with its own certificate store. It runs on the edge node(s) with host networking, so it sees real client IPs.
  • The UI is Flutter (web build embedded into the panel binary; the same code is the mobile/desktop app).

docs.title: License
docs.text: Source-available under the Nectar Source License: free for personal use and home labs, education and nonprofits, and small businesses (fewer than 100 people and less than $1M revenue). Commercial licenses: support@techbrain.llc.

docs.title: Users and roles
docs.text:
• Settings → Users invites people (by email, or a link to share) and gives them roles everywhere or per project. The first account is the Owner (every permission; there is always at least one active Owner).
  • Settings → Roles shows the permission matrix. Built-in roles (Admin, Developer, Deployer, Viewer) can be cloned into your own.
  • A project's Members card lets people with project.members add colleagues to that project.
  • Every change is in the audit log.

docs.title: API tokens
docs.text: Settings → API tokens: a token acts as its user, optionally limited to one role and one project, and can expire. Use them for the CLI, CI and the API (Authorization: Bearer nat_…).

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.text:
Settings → Sign-in providers adds buttons to the login page of the web panel:

Provider Setup GitHub GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → New; the panel uses the verified primary email Google Google Cloud console → APIs & Services → Credentials → OAuth client ID (Web application) OpenID Connect Authentik, Keycloak, Zitadel, Okta, Entra ID …: give the issuer URL; the panel reads its discovery document

For each one, register the callback URL the dialog shows (https://<panel>/api/auth/sso/<id>/callback) at the provider, then paste the client ID and secret (stored encrypted).

  • Without allowed email domains, only people who already have a user can sign in this way (matched by verified email).
  • With allowed domains you can create users on their first sign-in with a default role.
  • Group → role mappings (OIDC groups claim, e.g. nectar-admins=admin) are applied at every sign-in.

Sign-in uses the authorization code flow with PKCE and a one-time state; the provider's own MFA applies.

docs.title: Passkeys
docs.text:
Settings → Passkeys → Add passkey (in the web panel, with a recent Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox): the browser creates a passkey with Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello, your phone or a security key. On the login page, Sign in with a passkey then signs you in without email, password or authenticator code — the passkey is both factors. Synced passkeys (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password …) work on all your devices.

A passkey belongs to the panel's address: one created at panel.example.com does not work at http://localhost:8080 or another domain of the panel. The mobile and desktop apps sign in with a password. An admin who resets someone's two-factor authentication (or nectar-apps admin reset-mfa) also removes their passkeys.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication
docs.text: Settings → Security: any authenticator app, with 10 one-time recovery codes.

docs.title: Existing k3s server (adopt mode)
docs.text:
Nectar can move into a k3s server that already runs apps — without breaking them on the way.

sudo sh install.sh --discover          # read-only report: proxies, routes, TLS, and what migrates (✓ ⚠ ✗)
sudo sh install.sh --adopt             # backup → shadow install → verify → cutover (asks before each change)
sudo sh install.sh --status            # phase, plus hosts that still reach the old proxy
sudo sh install.sh --rollback          # the old proxy serves 80/443 again
sudo sh install.sh --finalize          # once nothing uses the old proxy any more

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: The report lists in-cluster controllers (Traefik, ingress-nginx, HAProxy, Kong, Contour, Istio, Cilium), proxies on the host (nginx, Caddy, Apache, HAProxy, a standalone nectar_gateway), who holds ports 80/443 and every route with its TLS setup, marking what migrates as is (✓), with caveats (⚠) or not at all (✗).

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
• migrate (default): nectar-gateway takes 80/443; the old proxy stays behind it as a fallback for anything it could not translate.
  • keep: your ingress controller stays; the panel writes standard Ingress objects for its apps.
  • adopt-gateway: import a standalone nectar_gateway.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• The backup covers the k3s datastore, routing objects and proxy configs.
  • The new gateway first runs on shadow ports 18080/18443 and is compared with the old proxy host by host (status, redirects, headers, body).
  • The cutover has a health gate and rolls back automatically.
  • Hosts that still use the fallback are counted; --finalize refuses to run while any host depends on the old proxy.

docs.title: Afterwards
docs.text:
• Ingress, Traefik IngressRoute and Gateway API HTTPRoute objects keep working: the panel syncs them to gateway routes, and cert-manager Secrets become gateway certificates. Synced Ingresses get the edge address in their status (kubectl get ingress, Argo CD health).
  • Existing namespaces show up read-only under External; adopt any of them as a project. The panel only manages objects it creates.
  • The built-in registry is not added unless you pass --registry (its mirror needs one k3s restart).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Checked every 30 seconds (Alerts → Rules sets thresholds and durations):

  • app or database down, crash loop, out-of-memory kills;
  • node not ready, high CPU / memory, disk almost full, volume almost full;
  • certificates about to expire, failed backups, an unreachable gateway, available updates;
  • events: deploy failed, deploy finished.

Each alert notifies when it fires and when it clears; optional reminders repeat while it keeps firing.

docs.title: Marking alerts as read
docs.text:
A firing alert shows on the dashboard and as a badge on Alerts in the menu. Once you've seen it, click ✓ (Mark as read) on the alert, or Mark all read on the dashboard card. The alert leaves your dashboard and badge but stays on the Alerts page, labelled read, until it resolves. Use the same button there to mark it unread again.

Read marks are per user: reading an alert doesn't hide it from your teammates. If the problem comes back later, it's a new incident and shows up again.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Channel ntfy your own ntfy server or ntfy.sh (pick a hard-to-guess topic); the ntfy app on your phone Telegram a bot from @BotFather and your chat id Email the panel's SMTP server (Settings → Email) or another one Webhook a JSON POST, signed with X-Nectar-Signature: sha256=<HMAC> when you set a secret Mobile app native push to the Nectar app (below)

Every channel has a Test button.

docs.title: Native push notifications (optional)
docs.text:
The Nectar app on Android, iPhone/iPad and Mac can receive alerts as native notifications through your own Firebase project (free tier). Tapping a notification opens the app or alert page.

  1. Create a project at console.firebase.google.com and add an Android app and/or an Apple app with the Nectar app's package name / bundle id.
  2. iPhone and Mac: create an APNs key in your Apple developer account and upload it under Firebase → Project settings → Cloud Messaging; enable the Push Notifications capability (and Background Modes → Remote notifications on iOS) in Xcode.
  3. In the panel, Settings → Push notifications → Set up: paste the service account key (Project settings → Service accounts → Generate new private key; stored encrypted with the master key), the sender id, and the app ids and API keys of your apps.
  4. Sign in to the Nectar app on your phone and allow notifications: it registers itself (Settings → Push notifications shows the number of devices; Send test to my devices checks the setup).
  5. Add a Mobile app channel under Alerts. Leave Users empty to notify everyone who can see the server, or list the emails of the people to notify.

The app needs no google-services.json / GoogleService-Info.plist: it reads the Firebase options from the panel after sign-in. Devices that uninstalled the app are forgotten automatically; signing out unregisters the device.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The panel's HTTP API is described by api/openapi.yaml (OpenAPI 3.1). Authenticate with an API token: Authorization: Bearer nat_…. Each endpoint lists the permission it needs as x-permission.

Download openapi.yaml

docs.title: Backups and recovery
docs.text:
Backups stores encrypted, deduplicated restic snapshots on S3-compatible storage (AWS, Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, MinIO), an SFTP server or a folder on the server.

A plan backs up the volumes of an app, a database dump or the panel itself (its database and uploads) on a schedule and keeps 7 daily, 4 weekly and 6 monthly snapshots by default. Any snapshot can be restored from the panel; a failed backup raises an alert.

docs.title: Rebuilding a lost server
docs.text:
Keep two things somewhere safe: the master key printed by the first install and the recovery kit of the target that holds the panel backup (Backups → target → Recovery kit). On the new server:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/minelifes/nectar_apps/main/deploy/install.sh \
  | sudo bash -s -- --base-domain apps.example.com --restore-kit kit.json --master-key 'KEY'

The panel restores its database first, then recreates the databases (with their latest dumps) and redeploys the apps (with their latest volume snapshots). A folder target on the lost server is gone with it — use off-site storage for the panel backup.

docs.title: Rotating the master key
docs.text:
sudo k3s kubectl -n nectar-system exec deploy/nectar-apps -- nectar-apps admin rotate-master-key

The command stores a new key next to the current one and restarts the panel, which re-seals every secret (environment variables, files, database credentials, two-factor secrets, alert channels, backup targets, registry logins, Git tokens, SMTP password, sign-in provider and push secrets) in one transaction, then makes the new key the current one. It prints the new key once: store it, download new recovery kits and take a panel backup — older backups still need the old key. --key K uses your own key (base64, 32 bytes); --no-restart leaves the restart to you.

docs.title: nectar.yaml
docs.text:
A project's apps, databases, variables, env groups, volumes, links and domains as one file you can keep in Git:

version: 1
env_groups:
  - name: shared
    env: { REGION: eu-central }
addons:
  - { slug: db, kind: postgres, version: "17", size_mb: 2048 }
apps:
  - slug: web
    image: ghcr.io/acme/web:1.4
    port: 8080
    env: { LOG_LEVEL: info, API_URL: "${api.url}" }
    secrets: { SESSION_KEY: "" }        # values are never exported; "" keeps the current one
    env_groups: [shared]
    links: [{ addon: db }]              # DATABASE_URL, PG* …
    volumes: [{ name: data, mount_path: /data, size_mb: 1024 }]
    domains: [shop.example.com]
  - slug: api
    image: ghcr.io/acme/api:2.0
    port: 3000
    replicas: 2
    health_path: /healthz
  • Export: project → ⋮ → Export, or nectar export --project shop > nectar.yaml.
  • Apply: project → ⋮ → Apply, or nectar apply -f nectar.yaml --project shop. Applying creates what is missing and updates existing apps; it never deletes anything.

Fields per app: slug, name, kind (web, worker, cron, task), runtime (image, java, node, …), runtime_version, image, port, internal_ports, command, args, replicas, cpu_millicores, memory_mb, health_path, schedule, release_command, env, secrets, volumes (storage_class), expose (extra TCP/UDP ports), domains, links (addon, prefix), env_groups.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Filled in at every deploy:

Reference Value ${db.DATABASE_URL}, ${db.PGHOST} … a database's connection settings (without linking it) ${api.host}, ${api.port}, ${api.url} another app of the project (internal address) ${api.SOME_VAR} one of another app's variables ${group.KEY} a value from a project env group

Workers with a port (e.g. MongoDB) and internal_ports are reachable by the project's apps at <app>:<port>, never from outside.

docs.title: One-click apps
docs.text:
Project → One-click app. Search the gallery or filter it by category, pick a template, name it and install it. The panel creates the apps, a managed database where one is needed, the volumes and generated passwords, then deploys them. After installing, the dialog shows how the project's apps connect (the *_URL to use).

Category Templates Messaging Mosquitto (MQTT), EMQX (MQTT with dashboard), Apache Kafka + Kafka UI, NATS (JetStream), RabbitMQ Databases Redis, PostgreSQL, MySQL (managed databases), MongoDB, Memcached, ClickHouse, InfluxDB, Qdrant Search Meilisearch, Typesense Monitoring Grafana, Prometheus, Jaeger, Uptime Kuma Developer tools Gitea, Mailpit, pgAdmin, Adminer, Verdaccio Auth Keycloak Websites, automation, storage WordPress, n8n, MinIO

Brokers and data stores without a login of their own (Kafka, NATS, Memcached, ClickHouse, Prometheus) run as workers, so only the project's apps can reach them. The MQTT brokers also open port 1883 on the server for devices; the node port is on the app's Overview. Tools with a web UI either have a login (Kafka UI, Mailpit, pgAdmin, Grafana) or say in their notes to restrict the domain with Allowed IPs (Jaeger, Adminer). nectar templates lists them and nectar install <template> --project shop installs one. The catalog is data (internal/blueprint/templates.yaml).

docs.title: docker-compose
docs.text: Project → ⋮ → Import docker-compose.yml, or nectar import-compose -f docker-compose.yml --project shop. Every service becomes an app with the same name (so services still find each other), services with published ports get a domain, databases and brokers stay internal, named volumes become volumes. Check shows the converted file and what could not be imported (bind mounts, build:, env_file).

docs.title: CI / GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Any CI can deploy with the CLI and two secrets, NECTAR_URL and NECTAR_TOKEN (a Deployer token limited to the project). For GitHub Actions there is an action:

- uses: minelifes/nectar_apps@v0
  with:
    url: ${{ secrets.NECTAR_URL }}
    token: ${{ secrets.NECTAR_TOKEN }}
    app: shop/api
    file: target/app.jar          # or: image: ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }}

Complete workflows (build a JAR and deploy it, build and push an image and deploy it) are in examples/github-actions.

Alternatively let the panel build: Git builds with a push webhook need no CI at all.

docs.title: Over HTTP
docs.text: Everything the panel does is available over HTTP with Authorization: Bearer nat_… (see the API reference). Large files can use the resumable tus endpoint POST /api/apps/{id}/uploads.

docs.title: The nectar CLI
docs.text:
install.sh puts the CLI on the server (/usr/local/bin/nectar, already pointed at the local panel, so nectar login only asks for a token). For your own machine, binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows are attached to every release; make cli builds it from source.

Create a token under Settings → API tokens (for CI: role Deployer, limited to one project).

nectar login --url https://panel.apps.example.com          # asks for the token, saves it in ~/.config/nectar
nectar apps
nectar deploy shop/api --file target/app.jar                # uploads, deploys, waits until it is live
nectar deploy shop/web --image ghcr.io/acme/web:1.4.2       # apps of the Docker image type
nectar status shop/api
nectar logs shop/api --tail 100
nectar rollback shop/api                                    # or --to 12
Command nectar login [--url URL] [--token nat_…] save the panel and an API token nectar whoami who the token belongs to nectar apps [--project SLUG] list apps nectar deploy APP [--file F \| --image REF] [--no-wait] [--timeout 15m] [--force] deploy and wait until live nectar status APP status, replicas and the live release nectar releases APP release history nectar rollback APP [--to N] redeploy release N (default: the previous one) nectar logs APP [--tail 200] the latest log lines nectar export --project SLUG the project as nectar.yaml nectar apply -f nectar.yaml --project SLUG [--no-deploy] create what is missing, update what exists nectar import-compose -f docker-compose.yml --project SLUG [--dry-run] [--no-deploy] convert a compose file nectar db list [--project SLUG] the project's databases nectar db connect DB [--project SLUG] [--port N] [--show-password] open a database on 127.0.0.1 through the panel nectar templates one-click apps nectar install TEMPLATE --project SLUG [--name NAME] [--set key=value]… install a one-click app nectar version

docs.title: Connecting to a database from your computer
docs.text:
Databases are only reachable from inside their project. nectar db connect opens one on your computer through the panel, with no SSH or open port needed:

$ nectar db connect vps/mysql
vps/mysql (MySQL 8.4) is on 127.0.0.1:3306 — press Ctrl+C to close
  user      app
  database  app
  password  (add --show-password, or Show credentials on the database page)
  connect   mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 3306 -u app -p app

Point any client at that address: psql, mysql, redis-cli, TablePlus, DBeaver or DataGrip. It uses the database's usual port when it is free, otherwise a free one (--port picks one). Each connection your client makes gets its own tunnel. It needs the permission to see the database's credentials, every tunnel is in the audit log, and the client still logs in with the database password.

APP is the app id or project/app. NECTAR_URL and NECTAR_TOKEN override the saved login (that is what CI uses). A rollback brings back the code and settings of that release; the app keeps its current number of replicas and its volumes.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
A project can run PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB or Redis next to its apps (project page → Databases). Each database gets its own volume and generated credentials and is only reachable from inside the project.

Link a database to an app and the app gets DATABASE_URL (or REDIS_URL) plus the usual PG* / MYSQL_* variables with its next deploy. A prefix such as CACHE_ lets one app use several databases (CACHE_REDIS_URL). Without linking, reference a single value anywhere: ${db.DATABASE_URL}.

Share with the whole project (database page → Overview) instead of linking app by app: every app in the project gets the variables, including apps you add later. Use a prefix when two shared databases would set the same variable (two PostgreSQL databases both set DATABASE_URL). If an app also has its own link to the database, the link's prefix wins. Like a link, sharing takes effect when each app is next deployed.

docs.title: Managing a database like an app
docs.text:
The database page has the same tabs as an app:

  • Metrics: CPU and memory over time, with the requested amount as a dashed line.
  • Logs: the live log of the database pod, with download.
  • Terminal: a shell in the database container, where psql, mysql or redis-cli are already installed.
  • Events: Kubernetes events, such as a failed volume mount or an out-of-memory kill.

Change CPU, memory and storage on the Overview tab. Storage can only grow. Restart restarts the pod; Stop frees its CPU and memory and keeps the data.

From your computer: nectar db connect project/db opens the database on 127.0.0.1 through the panel, for any client (psql, mysql, TablePlus, DBeaver…). See CLI.

Databases can be backed up (a dump on a schedule) and restored from the panel — see Backups.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Requirements: Go 1.26+. Everything else (Docker runtime, k3d, kubectl) is installed by the dev script; Flutter (via fvm) for the UI.

make dev-cluster                  # macOS: k3s in Docker (k3d)
make dev                          # starts the dev cluster + kubectl proxy and runs the panel
open http://localhost:8080        # setup token in dev mode: "dev"
make dev-cluster-down             # stop and delete the dev cluster

make ui-setup    # once: generate the Flutter platform folders
make ui-dev      # the UI in Chrome against `make run`
make ui build    # embed the web UI into the binary
make test        # unit + API tests
make lint        # go vet + gofmt
make shellcheck  # installer lint
make help        # everything else

Layout: cmd/nectar-apps (panel binary) · cmd/nectar (CLI) · internal/ (api, auth, authz, store, kube, deploy, routing, gateway client, alerts, backups, blueprint, sso, push, …) · api/openapi.yaml (API contract) · deploy/ (installer + manifests) · web/ (embedded UI) · ui/ (Flutter) · docs/ (this site, MkDocs Material: pip install mkdocs-material && mkdocs serve).

Contributions need the CLA.

docs.title: Domains and HTTPS
docs.text: Every web app gets a default domain, <app>-<project>.<base domain>, with a Let's Encrypt certificate. Add your own domains under app → Domains; point them at the server (or let the panel create the DNS records).

docs.title: Domains page
docs.text: Sidebar → Domains lists every domain of every app you can see with its project, HTTPS state, web options and DNS state; filter by "Custom" or "Problems", check DNS, and edit each row. The DNS setup card lists the records to create at your DNS provider (*.<base domain> and your own domains → the server's IPs).

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
• Per domain: the gateway obtains and renews a certificate over HTTP-01 (port 80 must reach the server).
  • Wildcard (Gateway → Certificates): add a Cloudflare API token (Zone:Read + DNS:Edit) and click Get *.<base domain>. One certificate proved over DNS-01 then serves every app subdomain: new apps have HTTPS at once, without per-app certificates or rate limits. Other wildcards work the same.
  • Upload your own certificate for a domain, or keep cert-manager (adopt mode syncs its Secrets).

docs.title: Automatic DNS records
docs.text: With a DNS provider in the gateway, switch on Create DNS records automatically: one *.<base domain> record covers every default domain, and each custom domain gets an A/AAAA record. Records are re-pointed when the server's IPs change (or when you add an edge node) and removed with their domain. Records someone else created are never changed (the domain shows "existing records").

docs.title: Web options (per domain)
docs.text:
In the domain dialog:

  • Redirect rules in order (/old → /new, /blog/… → https://blog.example.com/…, 301/302/307/308), and redirect domains (www ↔ apex).
  • IP allowlist: other clients get 403.
  • Headers: response and request headers to set or remove.
  • CORS: allowed origins, methods and headers; preflights are answered by the gateway.
  • Compression (gzip for text responses) and HSTS.
  • Basic auth, rate limit (requests/s per client; over the limit → 429, a client that keeps hammering is blocked for a while), upload size, timeouts, maintenance page, backend protocol (HTTP/1.1 or h2c for gRPC).

docs.title: Gateway page
docs.text: Server → Gateway shows every route with its health check, certificate and rate limit, the latest requests over all domains (filter by domain, status class or client IP; block an IP from its row), certificates and blocked IPs.

docs.title: Env groups
docs.text: A project's env groups (project page → Env groups) hold variables several apps share — a region, an API endpoint, a Sentry DSN. Apps pick their groups on the Environment tab (their own variables win); anywhere else, reference a value as ${group.KEY}. Changing a group marks its apps for redeploy.

docs.title: Copies and environments
docs.text:
• Copy app (app menu): settings, variables (secrets included), files, groups and links into a new app of the same project. It is not deployed until you deploy it.
  • New environment (project menu): clones the whole project — env groups, new empty databases with new passwords, and the apps — as e.g. shop-staging, labelled with its environment and linked to its origin.
  • Promote (app menu): deploys the live image or artifact of an app to the app with the same slug in the other environment (staging → production) without rebuilding.

docs.title: First deploy
docs.text:
1. Create a project (Projects → New). A project is a Kubernetes namespace with its own quota, members, databases and env groups.
  2. New app → pick a type (runtimes): Java (JAR), Native binary, Static website, Node.js, Python, PHP or Docker image; choose a version and the kind:
    • web — answers HTTP on a port and gets a domain;
    • worker — runs continuously without a domain (queues, bots);
    • cron — runs on a schedule;
    • task — runs to completion when you start it (migrations, one-off scripts).
  3. Upload the artifact (drag and drop; large files resume after a broken connection) or give the image.
  4. Deploy. The panel shows each step (pull, start, health check). The app is live at https://<app>-<project>.<base domain>.

Every deploy is a release: roll back to any earlier one (code and settings) from the Deploys tab.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Environment variables and secrets: app → Environment. Secrets are encrypted with the master key. Reference other apps and databases with ${api.url}, ${db.DATABASE_URL}, shared values with ${group.KEY} (environments).
  • Scale: replicas, CPU and memory limits, health check path (app → Settings).
  • Your own domain: app → Domains → Add (domains).
  • A database: project → Databases (databases).
  • Deploy from CI: CLI and GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Git builds and registries
docs.text:
An app of the Docker image type can be built from a Git repository (New app → Docker image → Build from Git, or the app's Settings): the repository URL, the branch and, for private repositories, an access token. The repository needs a Dockerfile.

  • Each build is a Kaniko Job in the project's namespace. It pushes registry.nectar.local/<project>/<app>:build-N to the built-in registry and deploys it. The Builds tab shows every build with its log; the newest 5 images per app are kept.
  • Push to deploy: add the webhook shown on the Builds tab to GitHub, GitLab or Gitea; every push to the branch builds and deploys.
  • Kaniko v1.23.2 is the default builder; set NECTAR_BUILDER_IMAGE on the panel to use a maintained fork: kubectl -n nectar-system set env deploy/nectar-apps NECTAR_BUILDER_IMAGE=<image>.

docs.title: Preview environments
docs.text:
Turn on A preview for every pull request in the app's Git source (Builds tab → Edit) and add pull request events to the webhook (GitHub/Gitea: Pull requests; GitLab: Merge request events). Then every pull request into the app's branch gets a preview:

  • an app <app>-pr<N> in the same project — a copy of the app's settings, variables, config files and env groups, with one replica — at https://<app>-pr<N>-<project>.<base domain>;
  • built from the pull request's head (refs/pull/N/head, GitLab refs/merge-requests/N/head), so pull requests from forks work too when you allow them;
  • rebuilt on every new commit, and deleted when the pull request is closed or merged, or after 14 days without activity (configurable, or never);
  • listed on the parent app's Builds tab with links to the preview and the pull request.

Databases: previews start without database links, so they cannot change real data. Allow Previews use this app's databases only when that is safe (e.g. a staging project). Forks: pull requests from forks are skipped unless allowed — their code would run with the app's variables and secrets. At most 10 previews per app run at a time.

Commit status: when the source's access token may write commit statuses (GitHub fine-grained token: Commit statuses: write; Gitea: write:repository; GitLab: api), the pull request shows nectar/preview — pending while it builds, then success with a link to the preview, or failure with a link to the build log.

docs.title: The built-in registry
docs.text: install.sh sets it up on new servers (--registry adds it to an existing one and restarts k3s once; --no-registry skips it). It is only reachable from the cluster and needs a password; nodes pull through a k3s mirror (/etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml). The installer manages only its own block of that file; if the file already has mirrors: or configs: of yours, it leaves it alone and prints the entries to merge.

docs.title: Private registries
docs.text: Images from GHCR, Docker Hub, GitLab or your own registry work with a login under Settings → Registries: every project gets it as an image pull secret, and builds use it for their base images.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A Linux server (amd64 or arm64): Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL/Rocky/Alma/Fedora, Alpine, Arch or openSUSE.
  • 2 CPU cores and 2 GB RAM are enough for the panel and a few small apps.
  • Ports 80 and 443 reachable from the internet, and a DNS name for your apps (e.g. *.apps.example.com → the server's IP). The panel can create the records for you on Cloudflare later.

docs.title: One command
docs.text:
curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/minelifes/nectar_apps/main/deploy/install.sh \
  | sudo sh -s -- --base-domain apps.example.com --email you@example.com

On a fresh server this installs k3s (without Traefik and ServiceLB), nectar-gateway on ports 80/443, the panel, the built-in image registry and the nectar CLI, and configures the firewall (ufw or firewalld).

At the end it prints:

  • the master key — store it somewhere safe; it decrypts every secret and is needed to restore backups;
  • an SSH tunnel command and a one-time setup link: the panel is not public until you create the first Owner account.

--dry-run prints every command without changing anything.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option --base-domain DOMAIN base domain for apps (<app>-<project>.<base domain>) --email EMAIL Let's Encrypt account email --admin-email EMAIL email of the first Owner --version V, --gateway-version V, --k3s-version V pin versions (default: latest stable) --skip-firewall leave the firewall alone --k3s-upgrades install Rancher's system-upgrade-controller so the panel can upgrade k3s --registry / --no-registry built-in image registry for Git builds (default on new installs) --longhorn Longhorn storage: volumes replicated across nodes (storage class longhorn) --nfs SERVER:/EXPORT NFS storage class nfs (volumes shared by several replicas) --join URL --token T add this machine to an existing cluster (the panel shows the full command) --restore-kit FILE --master-key KEY rebuild a lost server from its panel backup (Backups) --discover, --adopt, --status, --rollback, --finalize adopt an existing k3s server --no-cli do not install the nectar CLI --uninstall (--purge-k3s) remove Nectar (and k3s — destroys all workloads) -y, --yes do not ask for confirmation

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
Open the setup link (through the SSH tunnel the installer printed), create the Owner account, then the setup wizard asks for the base domain, the HTTPS email and offers a sample app to check that DNS, HTTPS and deploys work end to end. After that the panel is reachable at https://panel.<base domain>.

If something goes wrong: sudo k3s kubectl -n nectar-system get pods and sudo k3s kubectl -n nectar-system logs deploy/nectar-apps. Recovery commands (reset a password, clear the IP allowlist, …) are listed under Security.

docs.title: Add a node
docs.text:
Server → Add node shows a one-line command for another Linux machine: it installs k3s as an agent, joins the cluster and sets up the registry mirror (and Longhorn/NFS clients if you use them). Apps then spread over the nodes.

Each node card can:

  • stop new pods (cordon) and allow them again;
  • move its pods away (drain, respecting disruption budgets);
  • remove a drained worker from the cluster.

Draining the edge node, or the last node that could take the pods, asks again first: it would take the gateway or the panel offline.

docs.title: Several edge nodes
docs.text:
By default nectar-gateway runs on one edge node (label nectar.dev/edge=true, set by install.sh) — the node your DNS points to. To serve traffic from more nodes:

  1. Open ports 80 and 443 on the other machine.
  2. On its node card choose Serve traffic too (edge node).

The panel labels the node nectar.dev/edge-replica=true and runs a gateway replica there (DaemonSet nectar-gateway-edge, same image as the main gateway). A replica:

  • copies routes, certificates, IP blocks and settings from the main gateway every 5 seconds;
  • answers Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 challenges through the main gateway, so certificates are issued whichever node Let's Encrypt reaches;
  • is read-only and reports "not ready" until its first copy;
  • keeps its own rate-limit blocks.

The node card shows whether the replica is in sync. DNS records the panel manages then list every edge node (round-robin DNS). If an edge node goes down for long, choose Stop serving traffic so the panel takes it out of DNS. Needs nectar-gateway with the replicas feature (the latest release).

docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
Artifact apps need no Dockerfile: the pod's init container downloads your upload (a short-lived signed URL) into the pod, and the main container is an official runtime image. Deploys take seconds and there is no registry involved. A small optional pre-pull DaemonSet keeps the runtime images your apps use warm on every node (Server → Disk → Retention).

Type Upload Versions Image Java (JAR) an executable .jar 25 LTS, 21, 17, 11, 8 Eclipse Temurin JRE Native binary one executable (Go, Rust, C/C++, Zig …) Debian, Alpine, distroless, static matching base image Static website / SPA zip of dist/ or build/ nginx nginx (SPA fallback to index.html) Node.js zip with package.json 24, 22, 20 official node Python zip with requirements.txt 3.13, 3.12, 3.11 official python PHP zip of the site 8.4, 8.3 php with Apache Docker image an image reference, or build from Git — yours

The panel detects the type of an upload (markers such as package.json, requirements.txt, index.php, index.html, Dockerfile) and suggests it. The command, port and health check have sensible defaults per runtime and can be changed in the app's settings (e.g. JVM options as arguments, a start script for Node).

docs.title: Settings that apply to every app
docs.text:
• Port and health check (HTTP path or TCP), replicas, CPU and memory limits.
  • Release command: runs before the new version starts (e.g. database migrations); a failure stops the deploy.
  • Environment variables and secrets, env groups, linked databases.
  • Volumes (persistent disks) and files (config files mounted into the container).
  • Extra ports (TCP/UDP opened on the server) and internal ports (reachable by the project's apps only).
  • A web terminal into any running pod.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Secrets (variables, files, database passwords, tokens, provider secrets) are sealed with the master key (AES-256-GCM, a key per purpose); see rotating it.
  • Two-factor authentication with recovery codes; Settings lists your sessions and signs out the ones you don't recognize.
  • IP allowlist (Settings → Access): only the listed addresses or networks reach the panel. The panel refuses a list that would lock you out, and connections from the server itself or a private network (e.g. an SSH tunnel) always pass.
  • Email (Settings → Email): with an SMTP server the panel sends invitations, password resets and alert emails.
  • Isolation: each project is a namespace with network policies (only the gateway and the project's own apps reach its pods), resource quotas, and pods without privileges.
  • Gateway: rate limits per domain, automatic blocking of clients that keep exceeding them, IP allowlists per domain, basic auth, HSTS. The gateway's admin port is closed to the internet by the installer's firewall rules and needs the service token.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
k3s kubectl -n nectar-system exec deploy/nectar-apps -- nectar-apps admin reset-password --email you@example.com
k3s kubectl -n nectar-system exec deploy/nectar-apps -- nectar-apps admin make-owner --email you@example.com
k3s kubectl -n nectar-system exec deploy/nectar-apps -- nectar-apps admin reset-mfa --email you@example.com   # lost phone
k3s kubectl -n nectar-system exec deploy/nectar-apps -- nectar-apps admin clear-ip-allowlist                  # locked out

Report vulnerabilities privately to support@techbrain.llc.

docs.title: Databases stay "deploying", builds fail with "permission denied" (Ubuntu 26.04)
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • MySQL or MariaDB logs stop at "Switching to dedicated user 'mysql'", or MariaDB warns "Signal handler thread did not exit in a timely manner".
  • PostgreSQL shows no logs at all.
  • Git builds fail right after a successful RUN with "failed to execute command: permission denied".
  • The kernel log shows lines like this:
sudo journalctl -k | grep 'apparmor="DENIED"' | grep 'operation="signal"'
# … profile="cri-containerd.apparmor.d" comm="gosu" … peer="cri-containerd.apparmor.d//&unconfined"

Cause: on newer Ubuntu releases (26.04 with k3s 1.36), processes in a container can carry the label cri-containerd.apparmor.d//&unconfined. k3s's container AppArmor profile only lets the plain label send signals, so signals inside a container are refused. Programs that signal their own processes then wait forever: gosu, which official images use to switch from root to their user, and databases stopping their own threads.

Fix: rerun the installer (it keeps your settings and data). On Ubuntu 25.10 and newer, or when the kernel log shows these denials, it installs /etc/apparmor.d/cri-containerd.apparmor.d. That is k3s's own profile plus one rule that treats the stacked label like the plain one. It is loaded right away, so running containers recover without a restart:

curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/minelifes/nectar_apps/main/deploy/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- --yes

--apparmor-fix installs the profile on any distribution, and --no-apparmor-fix never installs it. Databases whose first start was interrupted may be half-initialized: delete and recreate them (new ones are empty anyway).

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Settings → Updates shows the versions of the panel, nectar-gateway and k3s and what is available. Per component choose off, notify only (default), auto: patch releases or auto: patch + minor, the channel (stable or beta), a maintenance window and how often to check. Major and breaking releases always wait for you.

An update runs in a short-lived Job, so the panel can update itself: it backs up the database, switches the image digest, waits until the new version is healthy (for the gateway also a canary and every route) and rolls back on its own when a check fails; a release that failed is not retried automatically. Panel and gateway are updated in an order that keeps them compatible, and Roll back in the history returns to the previous versions. Gateway replicas on extra edge nodes follow the main gateway within a few minutes. The web UI updates with the panel ("new version, reload").

k3s updates need Rancher's system-upgrade-controller (install.sh --k3s-upgrades); the panel then manages the upgrade plans (follow a channel in the maintenance window, or upgrade to a version now).

The panel reads a small updates.json feed published on GitHub Pages by each repository's release workflow and falls back to the GitHub Releases API.

docs.title: Volumes
docs.text:
• Add a volume (persistent disk) to an app with a mount path and size.
  • Files (app → Settings → Volumes → Files): browse a volume, upload and download files (up to 64 MB), edit text files, create folders, rename and delete — also while the app is stopped and for images without a shell. A small helper pod mounts the volume while the dialog is open (an hour at most). Needs the volume.manage permission; every change is audited.
  • Usage: each volume shows how much it holds: the app's Settings → Volumes, the database page and Server → Volumes. The Volume almost full alert (90 % by default) warns early. On the default local-path storage a volume is a folder on the server's disk. Kubernetes cannot tell a folder's size, so the panel measures these folders itself every 10 minutes, with a short read-only du pod per node. The numbers appear a few minutes after the panel starts. Sizes are not enforced on local-path: a volume can grow past its size until the node's disk is full, which is why the alert matters.
  • Storage classes: local-path (one node) by default; install.sh --longhorn adds Longhorn (replicated across nodes), install.sh --nfs 10.0.0.5:/srv/nectar an nfs class whose volumes several replicas on several nodes can share (shared volumes, ReadWriteMany). The class is chosen per volume and fixed afterwards; --join with the same flag installs the storage client on a new node.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: The Logs tab has Live (the stream of every pod) and History: the panel follows the pods itself and keeps their logs on its disk (7 days, up to 512 MB per app by default — Server → Disk → Retention). Search by text or regular expression over the last hour up to everything kept, also across crashes, restarts and deploys. History is stored per hour and compressed once the hour is over; deleting an app deletes its logs.

docs.title: Metrics and events
docs.text: App pages show CPU, memory and restarts per pod; Server shows nodes, disk and Kubernetes events. The gateway records requests per domain (status, latency, bytes) for the traffic charts and the access log.
